content.value: This document defines the target architecture for unifying ASAF and the existing market schemas into a composable master-plus-subschema model. The goal is to let analysts select a master operating model, choose one or more market bundles, dynamically assemble a working schema, and project vendor capabilities into that view without rescoring the same concept repeatedly across multiple frameworks.

Recommended principle: do not replace every schema with one giant taxonomy. Instead, separate canonical capabilities, schema bundles, vendor mappings, and delivery models so the platform can support reuse, traceability, future market-specific composition, and faster page loading even if JSON remains the primary storage architecture.

A JSON-first architecture remains viable if the platform stops treating a single large JSON file as both source-of-truth and page payload. The future state should separate source JSON from display JSON, use summary/detail/analytics payload tiers, and lazy-load page-specific content instead of loading full vendor datasets eagerly into the browser.

content.value: Current architectural constraints

items: Schemas are treated as separate source files rather than as bundles built from reusable canonical capabilities.
ASAF and APEF are handled through a special `asmf` branch rather than a generalized framework composition pattern.
Cross-schema reasoning exists today, but it is manual and hard-coded in Python instead of declarative and reusable.
Vendor evidence and score logic still live primarily inside schema-specific contexts instead of a normalized capability layer.
The UI can switch schemas, but it cannot yet compose multiple selected bundles into a single working view.
The browser currently loads full vendor datasets eagerly for core views, which increases page-weight and pushes filtering work to the client.
The backend rereads and reparses the same JSON files across multiple routes instead of caching parsed JSON by file and modified time.
Several views request metadata, field values, and full datasets separately even when those can be returned from a lighter summary bootstrap payload.

content.value: The target state is a master-plus-subschema platform. The master model defines the canonical capability graph and operating relationships. Subschemas are curated bundle views built from that graph. Vendors are mapped once against the canonical capabilities and then projected into whichever schema lens the analyst selects.

content.value: Design rules

items: Canonical capability IDs must be durable and non-market-branded.
Capabilities should be smaller than current pillars so multiple bundles can reuse them cleanly.
The ontology must support many-to-many relationships: one capability may map to multiple bundles and multiple ASAF dimensions.
Master-level relationships must be explicit, not inferred only from bundle grouping.

sections.title: ASAF as the Master Organizing Lens

content.value: ASAF should be treated as the primary master organizing lens because it already models how security operations function as an integrated system. It is the right frame for the operating architecture, but it should not force every market schema to adopt the exact same scoring semantics.

rows: It already models dimensions, sub-dimensions, weights, and stages
Use its dimensions as top-level operating-model anchors
Do not force every bundle to collapse into ASAF stage scoring
It describes how the system works together, not just what features exist
Map canonical capabilities to one or more ASAF dimensions
Do not require every bundle pillar to be identical to an ASAF dimension
It supports maturity progression and transformation paths
Preserve stage alignment as one score dimension
Do not replace market-specific capability scoring with stage-only scoring

Recommended long-term position: use a generalized master ontology with ASAF as the first and default master lens. That keeps the model flexible enough for non-SecOps-heavy domains while still making ASAF the practical control architecture for the platform.

Existing schemas should become declarative bundle definitions rather than standalone ontologies. Each bundle selects canonical capabilities, groups them into display pillars, assigns weights, and defines the scoring semantics and analyst framing for that market view.

sections.title: JSON-First Performance and Dynamic Loading Model

content.value: If the platform remains JSON-first, performance improvements should come from reshaping data delivery rather than replacing JSON outright. The most important design change is to stop using the same heavy JSON object as the source-of-truth record, the list-view payload, the analytics payload, and the detail-view payload.

rows: Vendor identity, top-level display fields, lightweight scores, sort keys, badges
Vendor table, initial dashboard, selectors, quick search
Full vendor evidence, rationale, granular scores, traceability objects
Vendor modal, deep-dive views, report tabs, exports
Precomputed aggregates, filter values, region counts, rankings, overlap summaries
Dashboard, cross-section defaults, market insight graphics, filter panels

content.value: Recommended JSON delivery rules

items: Load summary JSON first and render the page shell immediately.
Load detail JSON only when a user opens a vendor, report, or deep-dive page that needs it.
Materialize analytics JSON separately so charts and counts do not require scanning the entire vendor dataset in the browser.
Return filter-value JSON as part of a summary bootstrap or from a dedicated cached analytics endpoint rather than recomputing it from the full vendor file on every load.
Use stable IDs and refs so the UI can follow lightweight references to heavier JSON only when needed.

content.value: The platform future state is a composition-driven application rather than a schema-switching application. The future state should preserve multiple score types instead of forcing everything into a single 1-to-5 number. Capability strength, evidence confidence, bundle fit, and ASAF stage alignment are different analytical concepts and should remain distinct.

content.value: Every displayed score in the future UI should be traceable. Analysts should be able to click from a bundle pillar score to the underlying canonical capabilities, then to the vendor mappings, and finally to the evidence excerpts or rationale that support the score.

The migration should be incremental. Legacy schema mode and composed mode should coexist until the new architecture reaches parity. If major architectural work is happening at the same time, JSON delivery changes should be implemented in the same program so the future-state model is performant from the beginning rather than retrofitted later.

content.value: Pilot recommendation

items: Start with PreCyber and OffSec because their overlap has already been analyzed and they provide a useful pilot for deduplication.
Use ASAF as the master organizing lens during the pilot, but keep capability scoring separate from ASAF stage scoring.
Do not break current `SCHEMA_REGISTRY` behavior until the composed pilot can produce equivalent metadata and bundle views.
At the same time, split page delivery into summary, detail, and analytics JSON so the pilot proves both architecture and performance together.
A pilot master ontology can represent overlapping PreCyber and OffSec concepts without duplicate canonical capabilities.
One vendor can be projected into both PreCyber and OffSec bundle views from the same canonical mapping set.
The platform can display both master-lens alignment and bundle-specific scores without conflating them.
At least one hard-coded cross-schema translation workflow is replaced by declarative bundle mapping configuration.
The composed UI can show master selection, selected bundles, deduplicated capabilities, and vendor traceability.
Initial pages render from summary payloads without requiring full vendor-detail JSON up front.
Analytics views can load from materialized JSON rather than recomputing over the entire vendor dataset in the browser.
Parsed JSON caching eliminates repeated file reparsing for unchanged vendor, bundle, doc, and analytics files.

content.value: Architecture decisions

rows: Use a generalized master ontology with ASAF as the primary default master lens
Canonicalize atomic capabilities, not current pillars
Score once at the canonical capability level and derive bundle projections
Parallel-run legacy mode and composed mode until parity is proven
Keep capability score, evidence confidence, stage alignment, and bundle-fit as separate values
Keep JSON as the primary persistence layer, but split source, summary, detail, and analytics payloads instead of shipping one heavy file everywhere
Adopt summary-first rendering with lazy detail fetches and cached analytics JSON
Cache parsed JSON by file path and modified time; add browser cache metadata for stable responses

content.value: Success is reached when an analyst can select a master, select multiple subschemas, see a deduplicated working schema, inspect a vendor across those views, and trace any displayed score back to canonical capability evidence — while the platform still loads quickly because only the JSON needed for the active view is fetched.
